paraphrase: Dhṛtarāṣṭra asks Sañjaya: in the field of dharma (dharmakṣetra), Kurukṣetra, assembled and eager to fight, what did my people (māmakāḥ) and the sons of Pāṇḍu (pāṇḍavāḥ) do?

fidelity.note: Paraphrase read against the Sanskrit: faithful, nothing added or omitted that changes the sense, no later-school or modern reading; speaker, tags and links plausible. Only verse spoken by Dhṛtarāṣṭra; speaker right; 'dharmakṣetra' kept as the text names the place.

checks.note: Verse(s) located in the local Gītā text (700-verse numbering = CE); the passage matches the paraphrase.

notes: Opening verse of the text (upakrama); the first word is 'dharmakṣetre'. Commentators read the phrase 'field of dharma' in various ways (as a traditional epithet of Kurukṣetra, or as significant for the whole teaching); the verse itself only names the place so. māmakāḥ ('my people') are Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons; pāṇḍavāḥ are the sons of Pāṇḍu. This is the only verse of the Gītā spoken by Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Narrative framing verse: tags unmarked/general; standpoint 'ethical-social' only because the frame is the warriors' war situation.
alt_notes: The frame: the dialogue reaches Dhṛtarāṣṭra through Sañjaya's divine sight (cf. 18.75).

paraphrase: The method of meditation: the yogin should constantly concentrate himself, alone in a solitary place, with mind and body controlled, without expectation or possessions; set up a firm seat in a clean place, neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, deerskin and kuśa grass; sitting there with mind one-pointed, controlling thought and senses, practise yoga for self-purification; holding body, head and neck erect and still, gazing at the tip of the nose without looking around, serene, fearless, firm in the vow of celibacy, the mind restrained and fixed on me, sit yoked and intent on me; moderate in food, sleep, recreation and effort; when the controlled mind rests in the self alone, free from longing, it is steady like a lamp in a windless place; the mind stilled by practice comes to rest, and seeing the self by the self one is content in the self, knowing the endless happiness grasped by the understanding beyond the senses; this is yoga, the unyoking from union with sorrow; withdrawing the mind gradually by a steady understanding and fixing it on the self, one should think of nothing; wherever the restless mind wanders, bring it back under control in the self; the yogin with a calm mind attains the supreme happiness of contact with Brahman, sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, sees me everywhere, and regards the pleasure and pain of all as his own.
speaker: Kṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Chapter 1 sets the scene and the crisis. 1.1: Dhṛtarāṣṭra asks Sañjaya what the two assembled armies did at Kurukṣetra, 'the field of dharma'. 1.2–11: Duryodhana goes to his teacher Droṇa, lists the leading warriors of the Pāṇḍava army (1.4–6) and of his own (1.8–9), compares the two forces (1.10) and orders that Bhīṣma be guarded (1.11). 1.12–19: Bhīṣma and then the Pāṇḍava side (Kṛṣṇa, Arjuna, Bhīma, Yudhiṣṭhira, Nakula, Sahadeva and others) blow their named conches; the uproar rends the Kauravas' hearts. 1.20–27: Arjuna asks Kṛṣṇa to station the chariot between the armies; Kṛṣṇa does so and tells him to look at the assembled Kurus; Arjuna sees his elders, teachers and kin on both sides. 1.28–46: overcome by pity (kṛpā) and despair (viṣāda), Arjuna describes his bodily collapse (1.28–30), says he sees no good (śreyas) in killing kin and wants neither victory nor kingship (1.31–37), argues that destroying a family destroys the family dharmas, leads to varṇa-mixture, the fall of the ancestors and hell (1.38–44), and says it would be better to be killed unresisting (1.45–46). 1.47: Arjuna sits down in the chariot, casting away his bow, his mind overwhelmed by grief (śoka). The chapter's purpose, as it presents itself, is to state Arjuna's grief and his argument from family dharma, which the following teaching answers.

notes: The colophon title (commonly 'Arjunaviṣādayoga' in the vulgate) is not among this edition's segments, so it is not quoted. Arjuna's arguments of 1.31–46 are answered by Kṛṣṇa from 2.2 onward (cf. 2.11, prajñāvādān).

paraphrase: Chapter 2 opens the teaching. 2.1–10 (frame): Kṛṣṇa rebukes Arjuna's faintness and unmanliness (2.2–3); Arjuna restates his dilemma — he cannot fight Bhīṣma and Droṇa, would rather live on alms, does not know which outcome is better — and asks Kṛṣṇa, as his disciple who has come for refuge, to tell him for certain what is better (śreyas) (2.4–8); he says 'I will not fight' and falls silent, and Kṛṣṇa, as if smiling, answers (2.9–10). 2.11–30: the teaching on the embodied self (dehin): the wise do not grieve; the self was never not and will never cease; it passes through bodies as through the ages of life and as through garments; what is not (asat) has no being and what is (sat) no non-being; the self neither slays nor is slain, is unborn, eternal, uncuttable, unmanifest and unthinkable; even on the contrary view birth and death are inevitable; therefore do not grieve. 2.31–38: the argument from one's own dharma (svadharma) and honour: a dharmic battle is the kṣatriya's best good and a door to heaven, refusal brings sin and disgrace; fight treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike. 2.39: transition — the understanding (buddhi) given 'in sāṃkhya' is now given 'in yoga'. 2.40–53: the yoga of understanding (buddhi-yoga): resolute understanding is one (2.41); the flowery speech of those who delight in Vedic statements and seek heaven and power keeps understanding from samādhi; the Vedas concern the three guṇas, be free of them (2.42–46); your right is to action, not its fruits; yoga is sameness and skill in actions; the wise, yoked with understanding, abandon the fruit and are freed from the bondage of birth (2.47–51); when understanding passes beyond delusion and stands steady in samādhi, you will attain yoga (2.52–53). 2.54–72: Arjuna asks about the person of steady wisdom (sthitaprajña); Kṛṣṇa describes him: he gives up all desires and is content in the self, unshaken by sorrow and pleasure, free from passion, fear and anger, withdraws the senses like a tortoise (2.55–61); the chain from dwelling on objects through attachment, desire, anger, delusion and loss of memory to ruin (2.62–63), and its reverse through mastered senses to serenity and steady understanding (2.64–68); the sage is awake where beings sleep, is filled by desires like the ocean yet unmoved, and without 'mine' and 'I' attains peace (2.69–71); this is the brahmic state, reaching which even at death one attains brahma-nirvāṇa (2.72). The chapter's purpose, as it presents itself, is to answer Arjuna's grief and his request for the good, first by knowledge of the self, then by the discipline of action done with steady understanding, culminating in the portrait of the one whose wisdom is steady.

correction_log.new: Chapter 2 opens the teaching. 2.1–10 (frame): Kṛṣṇa rebukes Arjuna's faintness and unmanliness (2.2–3); Arjuna restates his dilemma — he cannot fight Bhīṣma and Droṇa, would rather live on alms, does not know which outcome is better — and asks Kṛṣṇa, as his disciple who has come for refuge, to tell him for certain what is better (śreyas) (2.4–8); he says 'I will not fight' and falls silent, and Kṛṣṇa, as if smiling, answers (2.9–10). 2.11–30: the teaching on the embodied self (dehin): the wise do not grieve; the self was never not and will never cease; it passes through bodies as through the ages of life and as through garments; what is not (asat) has no being and what is (sat) no non-being; the self neither slays nor is slain, is unborn, eternal, uncuttable, unmanifest and unthinkable; even on the contrary view birth and death are inevitable; therefore do not grieve. 2.31–38: the argument from one's own dharma (svadharma) and honour: a dharmic battle is the kṣatriya's best good and a door to heaven, refusal brings sin and disgrace; fight treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike. 2.39: transition — the understanding (buddhi) given 'in sāṃkhya' is now given 'in yoga'. 2.40–53: the yoga of understanding (buddhi-yoga): resolute understanding is one (2.41); the flowery speech of those who delight in Vedic statements and seek heaven and power keeps understanding from samādhi; the Vedas concern the three guṇas, be free of them (2.42–46); your right is to action, not its fruits; yoga is sameness and skill in actions; the wise, yoked with understanding, abandon the fruit and are freed from the bondage of birth (2.47–51); when understanding passes beyond delusion and stands steady in samādhi, you will attain yoga (2.52–53). 2.54–72: Arjuna asks about the person of steady wisdom (sthitaprajña); Kṛṣṇa describes him: he gives up all desires and is content in the self, unshaken by sorrow and pleasure, free from passion, fear and anger, withdraws the senses like a tortoise (2.55–61); the chain from dwelling on objects through attachment, desire, anger, delusion and loss of memory to ruin (2.62–63), and its reverse through mastered senses to serenity and steady understanding (2.64–68); the sage is awake where beings sleep, is filled by desires like the ocean yet unmoved, and without 'mine' and 'I' attains peace (2.69–71); this is the brahmic state, reaching which even at death one attains brahma-nirvāṇa (2.72). paraphrase: Chapter 3 answers the question of understanding versus action. 3.1–2: Arjuna asks why, if understanding (buddhi) is held superior to action, Kṛṣṇa urges him to terrible action, and asks for one decisive teaching. 3.3–9: Kṛṣṇa says he declared of old a twofold commitment (niṣṭhā) — the yoga of knowledge for the sāṃkhyas and the yoga of action for the yogins; actionlessness (naiṣkarmya) is not reached by not acting nor perfection by mere renunciation; no one can stay without acting, since the guṇas of prakṛti make everyone act; restraining the organs of action while the mind dwells on objects is hypocrisy, while karma-yoga with the senses controlled and without attachment excels; do your allotted action, for the world is bound by action except action for sacrifice. 3.10–16: Prajāpati created beings with sacrifice, telling them to nourish the gods and be nourished; who enjoys the gods' gifts without offering is a thief; eating the remains of sacrifice frees from fault; the wheel of food, rain, sacrifice, action, brahman and the imperishable must be kept turning. 3.17–18: for one who delights and is content in the self there is nothing that must be done. 3.19–26: therefore act unattached; Janaka and others reached perfection by action; act for the holding together of the world (loka-saṃgraha), since people follow the best; Kṛṣṇa himself, needing nothing, keeps acting lest the worlds perish; the wise should act unattached as the unwise act attached, and not unsettle the understanding of the ignorant. 3.27–29: actions are done by the guṇas, and only one deluded by the sense of 'I' (ahaṃkāra) thinks 'I am the doer'; the knower of the truth is not attached. 3.30–32: resign all actions to Kṛṣṇa and fight; those who follow this teaching with faith are released, those who cavil are lost. 3.33–35: all beings follow their nature; attraction and aversion lie in wait in the sense-objects; one's own dharma, though imperfect, is better than another's. 3.36–43: Arjuna asks what drives a person to sin against his will; Kṛṣṇa names desire and anger, born of rajas, the enemy that covers knowledge as smoke covers fire, seated in the senses, mind and understanding; restrain the senses first, know what is beyond understanding, steady the self by the self and slay desire. The chapter's purpose, as it presents itself, is to show why Arjuna must act — action being unavoidable, sacrificial, exemplary and non-binding when done without attachment — and to name desire as what must be overcome.
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
